## The question for today

When two datasets have been processed separately, how can we tell whether their columns still mean the same thing?

We will turn messy talk metadata into repeatable cleaning rules. String operations provide the hands-on example. We will then compare two versions of a pipeline and decide which results are compatible.

## Materials

- [Lecture slides](slides.qmd)
- [Download the follow-along notebook](follow-along.ipynb)
- [View the cleaning functions](cleaning.py)
- [Reference talk records](data/talks_reference.csv) and [new talk records](data/talks_new.csv)

The talk titles and word counts are invented for this lesson. The notebook and slides use the same data and fixed reference values.

## Run the notebook

Clone or download this repository, run `uv sync`, and open `follow-along.ipynb` in Positron with the project's `.venv` Python kernel. If Positron does not list the kernel, run the installation command in the local `README.md`.

## Today's route

1. Review missingness using the observation indicator $R$.
2. Predict the output of simple pandas string operations.
3. Write a function that cleans speaker keys and scales word counts.
4. Check the output, then inspect what changes when the processing rule changes.
